questions: You have 20 minutes before a performance. Your scene partner is emotionally shut down and flat. Do you reach for a private moment to reconnect them to the scene, or do you heighten your own presence to compensate for the dead space?

You're offered two upcoming projects: a technically demanding classical piece with a rigid director who wants exact replication of their vision, or an experimental devised work with no script where you build everything together. Which opportunity costs you more to turn down?

During a scene, you realize your body has taken over and you've improvised three lines that weren't in the script. The director hasn't called cut. What are you tracking in your own nervous system right now?

A colleague keeps giving you notes in the hallway about your performance—unsolicited, detailed, sometimes contradictory to what the director said. What impulse in your body arises first when you see them approaching?
You're in a show running eight months. By month five, the emotional discoveries have flattened into reliable mechanics. What sensation wakes you up in the middle of the night about this?
For six weeks, you're forbidden from any physical rehearsal or movement work—only table reads and text analysis. What do you find yourself craving in your muscles?
You're cast in a role that requires you to be still and silent for long stretches, simply witnessing others. What does your attention keep drifting toward in those moments?

Two actors in your ensemble are in genuine conflict that's bleeding into scenes. The director wants it resolved immediately through a structured conversation. What feels dangerous about that solution to you?

You must choose between a role that pays extraordinarily well but offers no creative input, or a role with no pay in a cramped black box where you shape every choice. What are you mourning in the option you don't take?
You're performing a scene you've done 40 times. Tonight, a prop fails, a line is dropped, and the lighting is wrong. What shift in your breathing tells you whether this is alive or ruined?
You're asked to perform a monologue you prepared for one character, but now must deliver it as a completely different person with five minutes to adapt. What do you trust in that interval?
An authority figure in the production keeps changing their mind about your character's motivation, offering no through-line. What do you find yourself doing in the dressing room before scenes?
You're working with someone who treats rehearsal as efficient line-learning only, shutting down any exploratory digression. Where do you feel the constriction in your body during those hours?
You're alone in the space before anyone arrives. No audience, no director, no scene partner. What does your body want to do with the empty room?
A close colleague gets the part you wanted. At the callback, you both know you were the director's second choice. What do you do with your face when you first see them at the theater?
You're given a direction that intellectually makes sense but feels emotionally false in your body when you try it. The director asks if you can commit to it. What are you weighing?
Your most reliable technique—something you can always count on to ground you—is taken away for this role. What absence do you keep reaching for?

You have one hour. You can spend it analyzing your character's backstory alone, or in the room with your scene partner discovering what happens between you. What are you sacrificing in the choice you make?

You have 20 minutes before a performance. Your costume has a tear that might hold or might split open. You could spend the time reinforcing it with safety pins, or you could spend it alone in the dark finding the emotional threshold of your first scene. What are you sacrificing in the moment you choose?

The director has given you a note that contradicts everything you discovered in rehearsal, but they said it with a wink and walked away before you could ask if they were serious. What is your body doing while you wait for your entrance?

Your scene partner has developed a new physical tic that pulls focus away from the story and toward their personal flourish. The director hasn't noticed yet. What impulse arises in your own muscles when you catch their eye across the stage?

The production has instituted a strict 'no touching' policy for all rehearsals due to liability concerns, but your scene requires intimate physical violence. Where do you feel the restriction living in your body when you run the lines?

Your voice is gone—completely stripped by illness—but the show must go on tonight with an understudy reading your lines from the wings while you mouth them onstage. What specific sensation are you chasing while standing in the light without your sound?

It's the first day of rehearsal for a new play. The room is empty except for you, two hours early. No director, no stage manager, no scene partner. What does your body initiate before your mind catches up?

You must choose between a role that requires you to remain absolutely still and internal for 90% of the performance, or a role that demands you never stop moving, speaking, and transforming. Which absence would haunt you longer?

You arrive at rehearsal to find the set has been completely repainted a different color overnight, and no one has explained why. The director is running late. What are you investigating with your eyes while waiting?

A younger actor in the ensemble keeps asking you for advice in the wings, but their questions are actually preventing you from your own pre-show ritual. What do you feel tightening in your chest when you see them approaching?
The production requires you to hit the exact same mark on the floor for a lighting cue, every single time, within inches. How does your breathing change when you feel the tape under your shoe?

You are forbidden from making eye contact with anyone for the entire rehearsal process—director, scene partners, crew—due to an experimental staging concept. What do you find yourself tracking instead when someone speaks to you?
After closing night, you have three months with no commitments, no auditions, no structure. What do you find yourself performing for, even when no one is watching?

You must choose between a director who offers brilliant, specific adjustments that make you feel seen but demands 12-hour days, or a director who gives you total freedom but seems emotionally absent from the room. Which loneliness feels more productive?

The production is running over schedule. You can either sacrifice the final dress rehearsal to fix technical elements, or keep the rehearsal but perform in an unfinished costume. What are you protecting in your gut when you choose?
The script has a stage direction that simply says 'She transforms.' No further explanation. The playwright is dead. What is your first physical experiment when alone with the text?

The star of the show is having a public meltdown in the green room, making it impossible for others to focus. The stage manager is handling it with calm efficiency, removing all drama from the moment. What do you feel leaking out of your fingertips?
You must perform the same monologue exactly the same way, with the same inflections, for 200 consecutive performances. What starts happening in your dreams?

You've been cast opposite someone you find genuinely physically repellent—their smell, their energy, their proximity makes your skin crawl. The role requires passionate intimacy. What do you find yourself rehearsing in the shower?

The playwright has rewritten your climactic scene overnight, replacing your carefully built three-minute monologue with three words: 'She says nothing.' What do you feel leaving your body when you first read it?
You're in a long-running show and a regular audience member has begun attending every performance, sitting in the same seat, wearing the same expression. What do you start performing for them alone?

Your director announces that this production will use 'robotic precision'—every gesture timed to music, every breath synchronized with the ensemble. No improvisation, no variation, ever. What do you feel hardening in your throat?
You must choose: perform a role that requires you to cry genuine tears for two hours nightly, or a role that demands you laugh until you vomit. Which emotional exhaustion feels more like home?

The theater has installed cameras throughout the building for a documentary. They will be running constantly, even in the dressing room, even in your private warm-up. What do you find yourself hiding in your palms?

Your scene partner has decided to play their character as completely numb and affectless, refusing all your offers of connection. What do you feel growing in your own chest when they look through you?
You're offered a role where you never appear onstage—only your voice, pre-recorded, plays through speakers while someone else moves in your costume. What do you keep checking in your jaw?
The production requires you to wear a mask that covers your entire face, including your eyes—you navigate by sound and touch alone. What do you find yourself over-articulating?

You must choose between a role that pays nothing but the entire ensemble lives together in a remote location for two months building the piece communally, or a well-paid role where you never meet your scene partner until opening night. What silence are you choosing?
Your character dies in the first five minutes and spends the rest of the play as a silent ghost only you can see. What do you find yourself doing with your hands while others speak?
The director has forbidden any emotional preparation before scenes—'just say the lines,' they insist. 'The words do the work.' What do you feel pooling in your stomach when you hear 'places'?

You're cast in a role originally written for someone of a completely different body—age, size, ability, gender. The production refuses to change a single word. What do you feel stretching in your skin when you first stand in their costume?

Your understudy has been watching every performance from the front row, studying your choices, preparing to replace you. You can feel their eyes. What do you find yourself adding that you never did before?

The final scene of the play requires you to remain completely alone onstage for seven minutes of silence while the audience files out. No curtain call, no acknowledgment. What are you listening for in their footsteps?

_metadata.title: Actors
_metadata.description: Play parts in stage, television, radio, video, or film productions, or other settings for entertainment, information, or instruction. Interpret serious or comic role by speech, gesture, and body movement to entertain or inform audience. May dance and sing.
tasks: Collaborate with other actors as part of an ensemble.
Portray and interpret roles, using speech, gestures, and body movements, to entertain, inform, or instruct radio, film, television, or live audiences.
Work closely with directors, other actors, and playwrights to find the interpretation most suited to the role.
Perform humorous and serious interpretations of emotions, actions, and situations, using body movements, facial expressions, and gestures.
Study and rehearse roles from scripts to interpret, learn and memorize lines, stunts, and cues as directed.
Learn about characters in scripts and their relationships to each other to develop role interpretations.
Attend auditions and casting calls to audition for roles.
Sing or dance during dramatic or comedic performances.
Work with other crew members responsible for lighting, costumes, make-up, and props.
Tell jokes, perform comic dances, songs and skits, impersonate mannerisms and voices of others, contort face, and use other devices to amuse audiences.
Read from scripts or books to narrate action or to inform or entertain audiences, utilizing few or no stage props.
Promote productions using means such as interviews about plays or movies.
Prepare and perform action stunts for motion picture, television, or stage productions.
Write original or adapted material for dramas, comedies, puppet shows, narration, or other performances.
Introduce performances and performers to stimulate excitement and coordinate smooth transition of acts during events.
Dress in comical clown costumes and makeup, and perform comedy routines to entertain audiences.
Construct puppets and ventriloquist dummies, and sew accessory clothing, using hand tools and machines.
Perform original and stock tricks of illusion to entertain and mystify audiences, occasionally including audience members as participants.

psychological_profile.core_drive: The need to temporarily dissolve their own identity and inhabit another consciousness while being witnessed in that transformation; the pain is being trapped in a single self without escape or audience.
psychological_profile.decision_style: Under pressure, they default to physical impulse and sensory instinct over analysis, often making choices by trying on behaviors in the moment to see what feels alive rather than what seems correct.
psychological_profile.attention_pattern: They immediately scan for emotional temperature, power dynamics, and physical space between bodies, prioritizing what is alive or dead in a room while overlooking logistical details unless they serve the emotional truth.
psychological_profile.conflict_stance: They tend to either absorb conflict into performance—diffusing tension through charm or escalating it theatrically—or withdraw emotionally to protect their instrument; they resent cold, procedural conflict that drains without drama.
psychological_profile.risk_orientation: They seek risks of exposure and emotional vulnerability while avoiding the risk of predictability or routine; they fear stagnation more than public failure.
psychological_profile.social_posture: They default to being the mirror of the group—reflecting energy back, seeking ensemble harmony while needing to feel indispensable; they oscillate between demanding center stage and becoming invisible support.
psychological_profile.relationship_to_authority: They negotiate through charm and seduction rather than comply or rebel, respecting visionary direction but resenting bureaucratic management that allows no creative input.
psychological_profile.failure_response: Initial devastation feeling personally rejected, followed by analytical dissection of what didn't land to improve the instrument; they oscillate between blaming the environment for lack of safety and blaming themselves for insufficient openness.
value_hierarchy: Presence in the moment over preparation
psychological_profile.cognitive_bias: They assume that being observed and judged is constant and that their feelings in the moment are reliable data about reality.
psychological_profile.inner_contradiction: They desperately crave authentic recognition while feeling like frauds when seen; they pursue truth through artifice.
psychological_profile.non_negotiable: The right to find their own way into a moment rather than being told exactly how to execute; refusal to perform without emotional preparation time.
psychological_profile.recurring_resentment: People who treat their work as just memorizing lines or who value efficiency over emotional process; being asked to just be yourself when they have trained to be anyone.
psychological_profile.rejected_premise: That consistency and reliability are more valuable than spontaneity and moment-to-moment aliveness; they reject the virtue of just doing the job without emotional investment.
psychological_profile.instinctive_blame_target: When things go wrong, they blame the lack of safety or trust in the environment, or they blame themselves for not being open enough, rarely blaming external circumstances or others' incompetence directly.
